---
title: "A differentiable surrogate likelihood"
---

This small CPU exercise checks the connection between an iTARFlow surrogate and
a caller's parameter-fitting code. It trains on a synthetic continuous bank,
saves/reloads the model, evaluates one held-out trajectory, and checks a finite
gradient. It does not fit a posterior or validate a scientific observation model.

## Run the complete example

In a METIS checkout with the development environment from
[installation](../basics/installing_metis.qmd):

```bash
uv run --locked --all-extras python examples/surrogate_likelihood.py --steps 20 --output likelihood-example
```

Or save [surrogate_likelihood.py](https://github.com/OJWatson/metis/blob/main/examples/surrogate_likelihood.py)
in your own installed uv project and run
`uv run python surrogate_likelihood.py --steps 20 --output likelihood-example`.
The example uses 24 parameter settings, three replicates and six timepoints,
with independent Gaussian noise added to a simple parameter-dependent response.
The short fit is an interface check, not evidence of likelihood accuracy.

## Use original units and preserve gradients

After loading the example artifact:

```python
import torch
from metis import Surrogate

model = Surrogate.load("likelihood-example/model.pt")
theta = torch.tensor([[0.5]], requires_grad=True)
# Supply your observed six-timepoint trajectory in the fitted response units.
observed = torch.tensor([[[0.5], [1.0], [1.5], [2.0], [2.5], [3.0]]])
log_likelihood = model.log_prob_tensor(theta, observed)
gradient, = torch.autograd.grad(log_likelihood.sum(), theta)
print(log_likelihood.detach(), gradient)
```

Inputs have shape `(batch, parameters)`, outputs `(batch, time, channels)` and
log densities `(batch,)`. The saved scaling is applied inside the method,
including its change-of-variables Jacobian. Do not manually normalize inputs
or observations first. `log_prob` provides the corresponding NumPy interface
when gradients are unnecessary.

## Where Bayesian inference would begin

For simulator parameters $\phi$, observed data $y$ and a separately chosen prior
$p(\phi)$, an approximate posterior could be defined by

$$
p(\phi\mid y)\propto p_{\mathrm{surrogate}}(y\mid\phi)\,p(\phi).
$$

The neural weights are fitted point estimates. Sampling the surrogate models
simulation variability; it does not integrate over uncertainty in those weights
or account for surrogate discrepancy. A deterministic surrogate combined with
an observation-error likelihood is a different model and must be specified as
such. Counts, exact constraints and real observations may require an explicit
observation model before this continuous density is meaningful.

Variational inference chooses a tractable distribution $q_\psi(\phi)$ and
optimizes an approximation such as the evidence lower bound,

$$
\mathcal L(\psi)=\mathbb E_{q_\psi}\left[
\log p_{\mathrm{surrogate}}(y\mid\phi)+\log p(\phi)-\log q_\psi(\phi)
\right].
$$

MCMC instead constructs a chain with the specified posterior as its stationary
distribution. Neither method repairs an inaccurate surrogate likelihood,
unsupported parameter regions or non-identifiability. Before implementing an
inference study, choose the prior and observation process, assess held-out
likelihood/calibration and surrogate sensitivity, then plan convergence,
identifiability and posterior predictive checks. These are future scientific
choices; this tutorial adds none automatically.

The original long VI/MCMC demonstration is available in the
[immutable source archive](https://github.com/OJWatson/metis/blob/739d57cdaa5f74b9a0973c527f063eaa3a72ab06/quarto/sbi/vi-mcmc.qmd).
Its raw-checkpoint and preprocessing recipe is historical. Follow the
[migration guidance](../package/migration.qmd) before reusing old weights.
